details:
**A Doll's House (Nora and Torvald Helmer)**
Ibsen's most famous play (1879), about Nora Helmer, who realizes her husband Torvald has treated her like a doll, as her father did before him. It ends with Nora leaving her husband and children and the famous offstage slam of the front door. Lucas Hnath's 2017 Broadway play A Doll's House, Part 2 imagines Nora's return.

**Krogstad and the forged signature**
Years before the play, Nora secretly borrowed money to take the seriously ill Torvald to Italy, forging her dying father's signature on the loan. Nils Krogstad, a disgraced employee at Torvald's bank, blackmails her with the forgery when Torvald plans to fire him. Nora's friend Christine Linde, Krogstad's former sweetheart, persuades him to relent.

**The tarantella, the macaroons, and the "little skylark"**
Torvald patronizingly calls Nora his "little skylark" and "squirrel" and scolds her for secretly eating macaroons. To keep him from opening Krogstad's revealing letter in the mailbox, she wildly rehearses the tarantella. The dying family friend Dr. Rank confesses his love for her.

**"The most wonderful thing of all"**
The ending of A Doll's House. When Torvald insists her most sacred duties are to her husband and children, Nora answers that she has "duties to myself," and she realizes she has been living with a "strange man" for eight years; this is their first serious conversation. She says that only "the most wonderful thing of all" could reunite them, and after she leaves, Torvald repeats the phrase with a flash of hope.

**Hedda Gabler**
Ibsen's 1890 play about Hedda, the daughter of General Gabler, who is bored in her marriage to the dull scholar Jørgen (George) Tesman. Seeking control over someone's fate, she manipulates those around her and finally shoots herself offstage with one of her father's pistols, after wildly playing the piano.

**Eilert Løvborg and the burned manuscript**
Tesman's brilliant rival and Hedda's former admirer, who has written a groundbreaking manuscript with the help of Thea Elvsted. When he loses it while drunk, Hedda secretly burns it, calling it his and Thea's "child," and gives him a pistol, urging him to die "beautifully," imagining him with "vine leaves in his hair." He instead dies sordidly when the pistol goes off in his breast pocket.

**Judge Brack**
The scheming family friend in Hedda Gabler who wants to be "the one cock in the basket" in the Tesman household. He recognizes the pistol from Løvborg's death and uses it to blackmail Hedda, who kills herself rather than be in his power. The play ends with his stunned line, "People don't do such things!"

**An Enemy of the People (Dr. Stockmann)**
An 1882 play in which Dr. Thomas Stockmann discovers that his town's new public baths, the source of its prosperity, are contaminated by waste. When he tries to reveal this, the town turns on him and declares him an "enemy of the people."

**The People's Messenger**
The newspaper in An Enemy of the People. Its editor Hovstad and the printer Aslaksen first promise to print Stockmann's article about the baths but back out after Stockmann's brother Peter, the mayor, warns that the cost of repairs would fall on the taxpayers and ruin the town's economy.

**Ghosts**
An 1881 play in which Mrs. Helene Alving learns that her son Oswald has inherited syphilis from his dissolute late father, Captain Alving, whose memory haunts the family. It ends with Oswald, losing his mind, repeating "the sun, the sun" as his mother screams, undecided whether to give him a lethal dose of morphine.

**The Wild Duck**
An 1884 play in which the idealist Gregers Werle insists on revealing truths to the family of Hjalmar Ekdal, destroying the "life-lie" that, according to Dr. Relling, makes life bearable. The teenage Hedvig, who is losing her eyesight, is persuaded to sacrifice the wounded wild duck kept in the attic where Old Ekdal hunts rabbits, but instead shoots herself. Gregers ends by saying his destiny is "to be the thirteenth at table."

**When We Dead Awaken**
Ibsen's last play (1899), about the aging sculptor Arnold Rubek and his former model Irene, who posed for his masterpiece "Resurrection" and now considers herself dead. The play ends when the two climb a mountain and are buried in an avalanche.

**Peer Gynt**
An 1867 verse drama about the boastful, wandering Norwegian Peer Gynt, who adventures among trolls and around the world. At the end the Button Molder comes to melt his soul down, warning they will meet at "the final crossroads," and Peer is redeemed in the arms of the faithful Solveig. Edvard Grieg's incidental music includes "In the Hall of the Mountain King" and "Solveig's Song."

**The Master Builder**
An 1892 play about the architect Halvard Solness, who fears being replaced by younger people. The young Hilde Wangel arrives claiming he promised her a "kingdom" ten years earlier, and she urges him to climb the tower of his new house to hang a wreath, from which he falls to his death.

**Rosmersholm**
An 1886 play in which Johannes Rosmer's first wife Beata drowned herself in the mill-race, driven to suicide partly by Rebecca West, who loves Rosmer. In the end Rosmer and Rebecca jump into the mill-race together.
